name: Reference-based or reference-free?
note: For each task, pick the grading approach that fits — and avoid the one that looks easy but breaks.

items.prompt: Grading a summarization model where many different phrasings are equally correct.
candidates: Semantic similarity or an LLM judge — exact match punishes valid paraphrases
Exact string match against one reference summary
items.correct: Semantic similarity or an LLM judge — exact match punishes valid paraphrases
items.explanation: With an open-ended target, a single reference is one of many right answers; exact match and n-gram overlap (BLEU/ROUGE) penalize correct paraphrases. Use embedding similarity, multiple references, or a reference-free LLM judge with a rubric — watching the judge biases from Chapter 7.
items.principle: When many phrasings are correct, don't grade by string overlap to one of them.

items.prompt: You have 50,000 production support tickets to evaluate answers on, and no gold answers.
candidates: Reference-free: an LLM judge on a rubric (faithfulness, helpfulness), anchored to a small human-labeled set
Skip evaluation — there's no ground truth
items.correct: Reference-free: an LLM judge on a rubric (faithfulness, helpfulness), anchored to a small human-labeled set
items.explanation: No references means reference-based metrics are off the table. Reference-free grading — an LLM judge on an explicit rubric, or grounded checks like faithfulness (Chapter 9) — scales, but must be calibrated against a small human-labeled anchor set so you can trust and monitor it.
items.principle: No gold answers → reference-free, but anchor the judge to human labels.

items.prompt: Grading math word problems that each have a single correct numeric answer.
candidates: Reference-based exact match on the final answer — cheap, exact, unbiased
An LLM judge scoring 1–5 for reasoning quality
Embedding similarity to a reference solution
items.correct: Reference-based exact match on the final answer — cheap, exact, unbiased
items.explanation: When there's exactly one right answer, exact match (or a verifier/unit test for code) is free, deterministic, and bias-free. Reaching for an LLM judge here adds cost and bias for no gain — save judges for tasks where no programmatic check exists.
items.principle: If you can check correctness programmatically, do — don't pay for a judge.
